title: "Is It Peace?"
sum: Elisha sends a young prophet to the army camp at Ramoth-gilead to anoint the commander Jehu as king of Israel, with orders to wipe out the house of Ahab. The officers spread their cloaks on the steps and proclaim him. Jehu drives hard for Jezreel, where King Joram is recovering from his wounds and King Ahaziah of Judah is visiting. Each rider sent to ask "Is it peace?" is swept into Jehu's column. On Naboth's land Jehu shoots Joram through the heart, and his men cut down Ahaziah as he flees.

Then Jehu enters Jezreel. Jezebel, her eyes painted and her hair dressed, meets him at the window with a taunt: "Is it peace, Zimri?" Her own servants throw her down, and when the men go to bury her, the dogs have left only her skull, feet and hands. Jehu reads it all as Elijah's word coming true. The chapter is a thriller, but it is also a study in prophecy, power and violence that the Bible itself will later question (Hosea 1:4).
readings: Read as judgment fulfilled

The narrator ties every death to a word of the LORD: Elijah's sentence on Ahab's house (1 Kings 21:21–24), Naboth's blood avenged on Naboth's land (9:25–26), the dogs at Jezreel (9:36–37). On this reading, Jehu is God's instrument, and the speed of the story shows the certainty of God's word.
Read as a political coup

Historians see an army revolt in a losing war, led by a commander who used a prophetic anointing, the grievances of the LORD's loyalists and a war against Aram to seize power. The Tel Dan stele suggests that Hazael of Aram claimed credit for the kings' deaths, which may mean that Jehu was allied with him.
Read as both

Many readers hold both together: God's judgment came through a ruthless man for mixed motives. Kings praises the act (10:30) but notes Jehu's later sins, and Hosea condemns "the blood of Jezreel" (Hosea 1:4). The Bible lets the reader see the cost.

views.H: The anointing fulfills the commission God gave Elijah at Horeb (1 Kings 19:16), and every detail of the deaths of Joram and Jezebel fulfills a prophecy. Traditional readers see God's justice for Naboth and the murdered prophets, carried out about 841 BC.
views.C: Most critical scholars think chapters 9–10 rest on an old, vivid account of Jehu's revolt, perhaps written to justify his dynasty, which prophetic and Deuteronomistic editors framed with prophecy and fulfillment (9:7–10, 9:36–37). Some see the anointing scene as a later legitimation.
views.A: The Tel Dan stele, an Aramaic inscription of about 840–800 BC, has its king, almost certainly Hazael, claim to have killed Joram of Israel and Ahaziah of the house of David. Shalmaneser III's records show Jehu paying tribute in 841 BC, the year of the coup. Excavations at Jezreel have found a large royal enclosure of the Omride period, destroyed in the late ninth century.
views.J: Jewish tradition named the young prophet as Jonah son of Amittai (Seder Olam; Rashi). The rabbis honored Jehu's zeal against Baal but blamed him for keeping the calves, and read Hosea 1:4 as punishment for that failure.
views.X: Christian readers have seen in Jezebel's fall a picture of the end of persecuting powers, as Revelation uses her name for a false prophet (Revelation 2:20), and in the cloaks on the steps a foreshadowing of Jesus' entry into Jerusalem (Matthew 21:8). Many Christian moralists, such as Calvin, held Jehu up as a warning: zeal for God mixed with ambition.

deep.b: Kings says Jehu shot Joram and his men struck Ahaziah (9:24, 9:27). The Tel Dan stele, found in 1993–94, has an Aramean king boast: "[I killed Jeho]ram son of [Ahab], king of Israel, and [I] killed [Ahaz]iahu son of [Jehoram, kin]g of the house of David." The names are partly restored, but the restoration is widely accepted. Athas, a minority voice, disputes how the fragments join, dates the stone later (about 796 BC, under Hazael's son) and reads it differently. Early doubts that bytdwd means "house of David" (Lemche, Davies) are now largely abandoned. Scholars have suggested four ways to fit the two accounts. (1) Royal inscriptions often claim credit for what happened in a king's wars, and Joram was wounded fighting Hazael (9:15). (2) Jehu may have been Hazael's ally, so that Hazael counted the deaths as his (William Schniedewind). (3) Kings may have given Jehu the credit to tie the deaths to prophecy. (4) The stone may simply be exaggerated. Chronicles gives yet another version of Ahaziah's death (2 Chronicles 22:7–9). No one solution is accepted by all.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the word "peace" as the chapter's verdict
deep.b: This is my own reading, building on the common observation that "peace" recurs through the chapter. The word shalom comes up nine times (9:11, 9:17, 9:18 twice, 9:19 twice, 9:22 twice, 9:31), and the question is never answered with a yes. I suggest the narrator means it as an ironic summary of Ahab's dynasty. Ahab's house had been promised disaster (1 Kings 21:21), and Jezebel had used the language of law and fasting to kill Naboth (1 Kings 21:9). When Jezebel herself asks "Is it peace?" at the end, she knows the answer. The prophets later attack those who cry "Peace, peace" when there is none (Jeremiah 6:14). If the reading is right, the chapter is not only a coup story but a sermon on false peace.

echoes: 1 Kings 19:15–17; 1 Kings 21:17–29; 1 Kings 16:9–20; 8:28–29; Hosea 1:4; 2 Chronicles 22:7–9; Matthew 21:8; Revelation 2:20

settings.what: Elisha's commission to the young prophet
settings.to: One of the sons of the prophets
settings.when: While Israel's army held Ramoth-gilead against Hazael, about 841 BC
settings.why: Detailed orders for a secret anointing: find Jehu, take him to a back room, pour the oil, run. The haste and secrecy show that this is a coup sanctioned by the LORD. For readers, it ties the bloody chapters ahead to Elijah's charge at Horeb (1 Kings 19:16).

settings.what: The oracle anointing Jehu
settings.by: The young prophet, speaking for the LORD, the God of Israel
settings.to: Jehu son of Jehoshaphat son of Nimshi, alone in the back room
settings.when: At the army camp at Ramoth-gilead
settings.why: To make Jehu king over 'the LORD's people' and give him a task: strike down Ahab's house and avenge the blood of the prophets shed by Jezebel. The words repeat Elijah's sentence on Ahab (1 Kings 21:21–24). Kings presents the coup as the LORD's justice, yet later prophets condemned the bloodshed at Jezreel (Hosea 1:4), so readers are asked to weigh both.
views: Kings itself: Jehu did what was right in the LORD's eyes against Ahab's house (10:30).

Many critical scholars hold that the story was shaped to justify the coup. Barré reads 2 Kings 9–11 as one narrative of political persuasion, probably written in Judah under Jehoash, to make the coups of Jehu and Jehoiada look legitimate. Hosea 1:4 judges the blood of Jezreel.

settings.what: Jehu's answer to Joram and his word over the body
settings.to: Joram king of Israel; then Bidkar, his officer
settings.when: On the plot of Naboth the Jezreelite
settings.why: 'What peace is there' names Jezebel's worship as the reason for the coup, and Jehu then recalls the word he heard with Bidkar behind Ahab (1 Kings 21:19). By throwing Joram's body on Naboth's land, he makes the killing a fulfilled prophecy. Readers see the LORD's justice for one poor man's field coming due a generation later.

settings.what: Jezebel's taunt
settings.to: Jehu, from her window as he came through the gate of Jezreel
settings.when: After Joram's death
settings.why: 'Is it peace, Zimri, who killed his master?' She calls Jehu by the name of a usurper who lasted seven days (1 Kings 16:9–20). The taunt is a queen's last challenge, and the words make readers ask whether Jehu's house will last.

settings.what: Jehu recalls Elijah's word on Jezebel
settings.to: The men who went to bury Jezebel
settings.when: After they found only her skull, feet and palms
settings.why: To declare her fate the fulfillment of Elijah's word (1 Kings 21:23). The narrator lets the usurper interpret his own deed, a reminder for readers that prophecy is fulfilled, though not always by good men.

title: Seventy Heads and a Temple Turned to Toilets
sum: Jehu finishes what he began. By letter he dares Samaria's nobles to fight for Ahab's seventy sons; terrified, they behead them and send the heads to Jezreel in baskets. Jehu has them piled at the gate and tells the people that the LORD's word has been done. On the road he slaughters forty-two princes of Judah, and he takes the strict Jehonadab son of Rechab into his chariot to "watch how zealous I am for the LORD."

In Samaria he announces a great sacrifice for Baal, packs Baal's temple with worshipers in special robes, and has his guards kill them all. The temple becomes a public toilet. The LORD praises Jehu and promises his sons the throne for four generations, but Jehu keeps Jeroboam's gold calves, and the LORD begins to cut away Israel's land through Hazael. Kings never mentions what Assyria recorded: Jehu bowing before Shalmaneser III.
readings: Read as reform

The traditional reading sees the end of Baal worship as the state religion of Israel, the triumph Elijah fought for on Carmel. Jehu's methods are harsh, but the narrator says God approved what he did to Ahab's house (10:30).
Read as power politics

Many modern readers notice how carefully the narrator shows Jehu's manipulation: an ambiguous letter that makes others do the killing (10:6), a speech that shares out the guilt (10:9), a lie to trap Baal's servants (10:19). On this reading, Kings lets readers see the gap between Jehu's zeal and Jehu's ambition, which is why it ends by saying he kept the calves (10:29–31).

views.H: Jehu fulfills Elijah's word against Ahab's house and destroys Baal worship in Israel. The four-generation promise is a real reward, and its exact fulfillment (15:12) shows God's faithfulness. His failure to remove the calves shows that political reform is not true repentance.
views.C: Critical scholars see an old account of the purge, perhaps from Jehu's court, reworked by editors who added the prophetic framework and the judgment on the calves (10:29–31). Some think 10:30 and 10:31 come from different hands, one praising and one blaming.
views.A: The Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III (British Museum) shows Jehu, or his envoy, kneeling before the Assyrian king in 841 BC, with a caption naming "Jehu son of Omri." Shalmaneser's annals record that he received tribute from Tyre, Sidon and Jehu that year. Hazael's conquests in Transjordan (10:32–33) fit the Aramean expansion seen in the Tel Dan stele.
views.J: The Talmud teaches that Jehu's pretended vow, "Jehu will serve him a great deal" (10:18), bound him, since "a covenant is made with the lips" (Bavli Sanhedrin 102a), and so he went on serving the calves. The Rechabites of Jeremiah 35 became a Jewish model of faithfulness to ancestral vows.
views.X: Christian writers have used Jehu as a lesson that outward zeal is not the same as a whole heart (10:31). His slaughter of Baal's worshipers has also been a test case in Christian debates about religious violence, and most modern Christian interpreters read it as a story bound to its time, not a model.

deep.b: This is the chapter's great question. The LORD tells Jehu, "You did a good thing when you did what is right in my eyes" (10:30). A century later, Hosea names his first son Jezreel, "In a very little while I will bring the blood shed at Jezreel down on the house of Jehu" (Hosea 1:4). Answers include: (1) Jehu was commanded to destroy Ahab's house, but he went beyond his commission, killing Ahaziah and forty-two princes of Judah, and acted for himself rather than for God (Calvin on Hosea 1:4); (2) the same acts were righteous when done and became guilt because Jehu did not walk with a whole heart (10:31), the view of Rashi and Radak on Hosea 1:4; (3) Hosea's "blood of Jezreel" refers to all the dynasty's violence, including later royal murders; (4) Hosea and Kings simply judge differently, and the canon keeps both. Whatever the answer, the Bible does not let the reader celebrate Jehu without asking.

Found by Austen Henry Layard at Nimrud in 1846, the Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III has five rows of carved panels showing tribute bearers. The second row shows a bearded man in a pointed cap prostrate before the king, with servants carrying gifts. The caption calls it "the tribute of Jehu son of Omri." "Son of Omri" means "of the house of Omri," Assyria's name for Israel, ironically applied to the man who wiped out Omri's family. Kings says nothing of the tribute; it speaks only of "all his strength" (10:34).

echoes: 1 Kings 21:21–24; 1 Kings 18:40; Numbers 25:11–13; Jeremiah 35:1–19; Hosea 1:4; Amos 1:3; Judges 9:5; 15:12

settings.what: Jehu's letters to Samaria and the leaders' reply
settings.by: Jehu; the palace steward, the city governor, the elders and the guardians
settings.to: The officials and elders of Samaria and the guardians of Ahab's sons; and back to Jehu
settings.when: Right after the deaths of Joram and Jezebel
settings.why: The first letter dares the leaders to crown one of Ahab's sons and fight. Their reply submits, and the second letter asks for the sons' heads. The letters show how Jehu made others share the guilt of the killing. Readers see the fear and politics behind the fulfilling of a prophecy.

settings.what: Jehu's speech at the gate of Jezreel
settings.to: All the people of Jezreel, beside the heaps of heads
settings.when: The morning after the heads arrived
settings.why: 'You are in the right... but all these, who struck them down?' Jehu admits killing his master but shifts the slaughter of the seventy onto Samaria's leaders, and he calls it all the LORD's word through Elijah. The speech is political and pious at once. Readers are left to judge its honesty.

settings.what: Jehu's words to Jehonadab
settings.to: Jehonadab son of Rechab, on the road to Samaria
settings.when: On Jehu's way to Samaria
settings.why: 'Watch how zealous I am for the LORD.' Jehu wins the backing of a strict follower of the LORD, whose clan later appears in Jeremiah 35. The boast of zeal invites readers to compare Jehu with Elijah, and the chapter's end shows his zeal stopped short at Jeroboam's calves.

settings.what: Jehu's call to a great sacrifice for Baal
settings.to: All the people; then all Baal's prophets, servants and priests; then his guards
settings.when: After he came to Samaria
settings.why: A deliberate trick: Jehu says he will serve Baal more than Ahab did, gathers every worshiper of Baal into one house, and has them killed. The narrator says plainly it was a trick. For readers the story explains how Baal worship ended in Israel, while 10:29–31 shows that the sins of Jeroboam remained.

settings.what: The LORD's word to Jehu
settings.to: Jehu
settings.when: After the end of Baal worship in Samaria
settings.why: To reward what Jehu did against Ahab's house with four generations on the throne. The promise frames the next chapters and is fulfilled in 15:12. It shows readers that the LORD can use and reward a flawed king while still judging what he left undone (10:31).

title: The Hidden King
sum: When Athaliah, Ahab's daughter and mother of the dead Ahaziah, hears of her son's death, she wipes out the royal family of Judah and takes the throne. Only one baby, Joash, escapes, hidden by his aunt Jehosheba in a storeroom and then in the temple for six years. David's line, and God's promise to David, hang on one hidden child.

In the seventh year the priest Jehoiada makes a pact with the royal guard. On a Sabbath, with the guard doubled at the changing of shifts, he brings out the seven-year-old, crowns him and gives him "the testimony." Athaliah runs in crying "Conspiracy!" and is taken out and killed at the horses' gate. Jehoiada renews the covenant between the LORD, the king and the people, and the people tear down Baal's temple in Jerusalem.
readings: Read as the rescue of David's line

The chapter shows God keeping his promise that David's house would never be without a lamp (1 Kings 11:36). The child hidden from a murderous ruler recalls Moses and, for Christians, the child Jesus hidden from Herod.
Read as a priestly revolution

Historians note that the coup is organized by the chief priest, carried out by palace guards and backed by "the people of the land." It restores the Davidic line, but it also makes the temple and its priests kingmakers, a power Chronicles develops further (2 Chronicles 23).

views.H: Athaliah's six-year reign (about 841–835 BC) is the low point of Judah's monarchy; the boy's survival is God's providence. Jehoiada acts as a faithful priest, and the covenant renewal sets Judah right with God.
views.C: Many scholars see two sources: an account of the coup centered on the guards (11:4–12, 11:18b–20) and one centered on the people and the covenant (11:13–18a). The covenant language is often attributed to Deuteronomistic editors.
views.A: No outside text mentions Athaliah, but the Tel Dan stele's claim to have killed Ahaziah "of the house of David" belongs to the same months. Carian mercenaries (11:4) are well attested in the seventh and sixth centuries; their presence in ninth-century Jerusalem is debated, and some read "Carites" as another name for the old royal guard.
views.J: Jewish tradition remembered Athaliah as the queen who nearly ended David's line. Rashi, drawing on Seder Olam, says Joash was hidden in the attic above the Holy of Holies, and reads Psalm 27:5, "he will hide me in the hidden part of his tent," in that light (Rashi on Psalm 27:5).
views.X: Christian readers saw in Joash, hidden in God's house and revealed as king, a picture of Christ, the Son of David kept safe from Herod (Matthew 2:13–16) and revealed in God's time. The Davidic line runs through Joash to Jesus, though Matthew's genealogy skips him (Matthew 1:8). Racine's play Athalie (1691), written for the girls of Saint-Cyr, made Joash's rescue famous in European literature, and Handel set it as an oratorio (1733).

deep.b: Athaliah is the only woman who ruled Israel or Judah in her own right in the biblical period (Salome Alexandra ruled Judea from 76 to 67 BC); Jezebel's power under Ahab and Jehoram was of a different kind. Kings tells her story entirely from her enemies' side and gives her no regnal formula. Some modern scholars suggest that, after Jehu's purge killed her son, mother, brother and forty-two princes, she acted to save herself and the Omride party in Judah, and that she may not have killed her own grandchildren but rival branches of the royal family. Others note that a woman's rule was so unusual that it could only end in a coup. None of this excuses the massacre the text describes, but it reminds readers that ancient royal histories were written by the winners.

Matthew lists "Joram fathered Uzziah" (Matthew 1:8), skipping Ahaziah, Joash and Amaziah. Many think Matthew left out three generations to make his three groups of fourteen (Matthew 1:17), and perhaps chose these because of their link to Athaliah and the house of Ahab; Christian commentators have discussed the omission since antiquity (Hilary; Jerome on Matthew 1:8).

echoes: 2 Chronicles 22:10–23:21; 2 Samuel 7:12–16; 1 Kings 11:36; Exodus 2:1–10; Deuteronomy 17:18–19; Matthew 1:8; Matthew 2:13–16

settings.what: Jehoiada's orders to the guard
settings.to: The officers over the hundreds of the Carites and the runners, sworn to a covenant in the LORD's house
settings.when: In the seventh year of Athaliah's rule, about 835 BC, on a Sabbath at the change of the guard
settings.why: Battle orders for a coup: post the shifts so that the boy king is ringed with armed men in the Temple. In Kings the guards are the royal bodyguard, and the plan is told as a careful military action. The point for readers is that David's line, down to one hidden child, was kept alive (8:19).

settings.what: The acclamation of Joash
settings.to: Joash, crowned and given the testimony
settings.when: At the pillar in the LORD's house
settings.why: 'Long live the king!' is the people's public consent to a new king of David's line. For readers who lived without a king, it recalled what the restoration of David's house would look like.

settings.what: Jehoiada's covenant
settings.to: The LORD, the king and the people; and the king and the people
settings.when: After Athaliah was killed
settings.why: Two covenants: one making king and people 'a people belonging to the LORD,' and one between the king and the people. They bind a seven-year-old king to the LORD and to his subjects, and lead at once to the pulling down of Baal's house. For readers, covenant renewal is the path back after a time of false worship, as in Josiah's day (23:3).

title: A Chest by the Altar
sum: Joash, now king, does what is right as long as the priest Jehoiada guides him. He orders the priests to use the temple's income for repairs, but twenty-three years later nothing has been fixed. So Jehoiada sets a chest with a hole in its lid beside the altar. The money goes straight to carpenters, builders and stonecutters, who work so honestly that no one asks them for receipts.

Then Hazael of Aram takes Gath and turns toward Jerusalem. Joash buys him off with all the holy gifts of his ancestors and the gold of the temple and palace. In the end his own servants murder him. Kings tells the story briefly and without comment; Chronicles adds a darker account of his later years and the stoning of Jehoiada's son Zechariah (2 Chronicles 24:17–22).
readings: Read as a story of temple care
The chapter honors the king who restored the LORD's house and the workmen who served it faithfully. It becomes a model for Josiah's repairs (22:3–7) and for honest handling of sacred money.
Read as a story of decline

Read with Chronicles, Joash's reign turns from promise to apostasy: the king saved in the temple ends by robbing it and, in Chronicles, by killing the priest's son there. Kings hints at the same arc by ending with the payment to Hazael and the murder.

views.H: Joash's long reign (about 835–796 BC) shows the good that a faithful mentor can do and the danger of faith that depends on someone else. The repairs are real history from temple records.
views.C: Scholars think 12:4–16 comes from a temple source, perhaps the same archive that lies behind 22:3–7. The two accounts share so much wording that some think one was modeled on the other.
views.A: Excavations at Tell es-Safi (Gath) have uncovered a siege trench around the city and a destruction dated to the late ninth century BC, widely connected with Hazael (12:17). The "Jehoash Inscription," a stone claiming to be Joash's own record of the repairs, appeared on the antiquities market in 2003 and is judged a forgery by most experts.
views.J: Jehoiada's chest was remembered in the Second Temple, where the Mishnah describes thirteen trumpet-shaped chests for offerings (Mishnah Shekalim 6:5). The Talmud tells that the blood of Zechariah son of Jehoiada kept bubbling until the Babylonian conquest (Bavli Gittin 57b).
views.X: Jesus speaks of the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, killed between the sanctuary and the altar (Matthew 23:35). He is usually taken to be Zechariah son of Jehoiada of 2 Chronicles 24, the last martyr in the Hebrew Bible's order of books. Christian preachers used Jehoiada's chest as a model of giving.

deep.b: Kings tells Joash's reign in twenty-two verses (11:21–12:21): the repairs, the tribute to Hazael and the murder. Chronicles has a fuller story (2 Chronicles 24). After Jehoiada dies, aged 130, the leaders of Judah persuade Joash to serve the Asherah poles. Jehoiada's son Zechariah warns them and is stoned "in the courtyard of the LORD's house" at the king's command. His dying words are "May the LORD see it, and may he seek it out" (2 Chronicles 24:22). Within a year a small Aramean army defeats Judah, Joash is wounded, and his servants kill him on his bed "over the blood of the sons of Jehoiada the priest" (2 Chronicles 24:25). Historians debate whether Chronicles had another source or explained Joash's disasters by its own theology of reward and punishment.

echoes: 2 Chronicles 24:1–27; 22:3–7; Exodus 30:12–16; Leviticus 27:2–8; Mark 12:41–44; Matthew 23:35; Luke 11:51

settings.what: Jehoash's orders on the Temple money
settings.to: The priests, and later Jehoiada and the priests
settings.when: Early in his reign; and again in his twenty-third year, about 813 BC
settings.why: Rules on Temple income: census money, vow money and freewill gifts go to repairs. When the priests did not fix the house, the king took the money out of their hands. The orders show a king of David's line caring for the LORD's house, and they explain the chest system that follows. Exiles who remembered the Temple, and later builders of a new one, could read it as a model of honest giving.

title: Arrows from a Dying Prophet
sum: Jehu's son Jehoahaz and grandson Jehoash reign in Israel under Aram's heel; Hazael has ground Israel's army down to ten chariots. Even so, when Jehoahaz pleads, the LORD sends "someone to save them," and the narrator stresses that God has not yet cast Israel off, for the sake of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

The center of the chapter is Elisha's last scene. King Jehoash weeps over the dying prophet with the cry Elisha once raised over Elijah. Elisha has him shoot an arrow east, "an arrow of the LORD's saving help," and strike the ground, but the king stops at three. After Elisha's burial, a dead man thrown into his grave comes back to life at the touch of his bones. Jehoash beats Ben-hadad three times, exactly as the prophet said.
readings: Read as prophecy and grace
God's mercy outlasts Israel's sins: he hears an evil king, sends a deliverer and keeps his covenant with the patriarchs. Elisha's power continues even after death, and his last word comes true.
Read as history with legend
Historians place Israel's recovery about 800 BC, when Assyria under Adad-nirari III weakened Damascus. The story of the bones is often read as a prophetic legend honoring Elisha.

views.H: The deliverer of 13:5 is God's gift in answer to prayer, whether Jehoash, Jeroboam II or another. Elisha's death and the miracle at his grave close the great prophetic era of Elijah and Elisha, about 795 BC.
views.C: Critical scholars think the Elisha stories (13:14–21) once stood with chapters 2–8 and were placed here because Elisha died under Jehoash. 13:4–6 and 13:23 are often attributed to an editor who saw Israel's history through the pattern of Judges.
views.A: Adad-nirari III's Tell al-Rimah stela lists "Joash of Samaria" among those who paid him tribute about 796 BC, the year he besieged Damascus. The Zakkur inscription names "Bar-hadad son of Hazael" leading a coalition against Hamath. Inscriptions from Kuntillet 'Ajrud of about 800 BC invoke "YHWH of Samaria and his asherah," matching 13:6.
views.J: The Talmud discusses the man raised at Elisha's grave and teaches that he lived only long enough to stand, because a wicked man should not lie beside a righteous one (Bavli Sanhedrin 47a). Ben Sira praises Elisha because even in death his body prophesied (Sirach 48:13–14).
views.X: Church fathers such as Cyril of Jerusalem cited the bones of Elisha in defense of honoring the relics of saints and as a sign of the resurrection. The cry "My father, my father!" has been read as a confession that the prophet's word, not armies, protects God's people.

deep.title: Claude's theory: two deaths that frame Elisha's career
deep.b: This is my own reading, though it builds on the widely noticed repetition of 2:12 in 13:14. Elisha's career begins with Elijah taken up alive, no body left behind, and Elisha crying "My father! My father! Israel's chariots and riders!" (2:12). It ends with Elisha dying of illness and buried, and a king saying the same words over him (13:14). The contrast seems deliberate: Elijah left no grave; Elisha's grave gives life (13:21). If so, the narrator is not ranking the two prophets but showing two ways God's power outlives his servants: one by taking the prophet away, the other by working through what is left of him. Elisha, who asked for a double share of Elijah's spirit (2:9), performs one last miracle that Elijah never did. Here my reading overlaps a well-known Jewish tradition that counts Elisha's miracles as twice Elijah's, with the raising at the grave completing the double share.

echoes: 2:12; 6:17; Judges 2:11–19; Judges 3:9; Exodus 2:24; Leviticus 26:42; Sirach 48:12–14; 1 Kings 20:26–30

settings.what: Elisha's last sign and oracle
settings.to: Jehoash king of Israel, who wept over him
settings.when: During Elisha's last illness, about 798 BC
settings.why: The king cries 'Israel's chariots and its riders!' as Elisha once cried over Elijah. Elisha has him shoot an arrow east, 'an arrow of the LORD's saving help,' and strike the ground. The king stops at three, and so will win only three times. The sign teaches that the LORD's help is received by bold trust. For later readers it also explains why Israel's recovery under Jehoash was real but limited (13:25).

traditions.q: A dead man came to life when his body touched Elisha's bones (2 Kings 13:21). Should Christians honor the relics of saints?
views: Yes. Cyril of Jerusalem cited this verse to show that God's power works even through the bodies of the saints (Catechetical Lectures 18.16). The Council of Trent taught that the bodies of martyrs and saints are to be honored (Session 25, 1563), and the Catechism counts relics among the Church's forms of devotion (Catechism 1674).

Yes. The Second Council of Nicaea (787) ordered that relics be placed in every church that is consecrated, and the faithful kiss them with reverence. The honor given to the saints is not the worship that belongs to God alone.

Luther called the trade in relics a fraud that drew people away from Christ (Smalcald Articles II.2), and the Augsburg Confession rejects calling on the saints (article 21). Lutherans remember the saints with thanks, but their bones carry no special grace.

No. Calvin's Treatise on Relics (1543) mocked the false relics of his day and warned that honoring bones leads to idolatry. The miracle at Elisha's grave was a single sign from God, not a command to keep or honor his remains.

Article 22 calls the Roman teaching on the worship of relics a foolish thing, vainly invented and against Scripture. Anglicans are divided in practice: some Anglo-Catholic parishes keep and honor relics.

title: The Thornbush and the Cedar
sum: In Judah, Amaziah takes revenge on his father's murderers but spares their sons, obeying the law of Moses, and crushes Edom in the Valley of Salt. Flushed with victory, he challenges Jehoash of Israel, who answers with a fable: a thornbush asked a cedar for its daughter and was trampled by a passing animal. Amaziah will not listen. Israel routs Judah at Beth-shemesh, captures Amaziah, breaks down Jerusalem's wall and loots the temple. Later Amaziah too is murdered.

In Israel, Jeroboam II reigns forty-one years and wins back Israel's old borders from Lebo-hamath to the Dead Sea, as the prophet Jonah son of Amittai had foretold. The narrator explains why God helped an evil king: the LORD saw Israel's bitter misery, and he had never said he would wipe out Israel's name.
readings: Read as pride before a fall
Amaziah's story is a lesson in the danger of success, told through Jehoash's fable and its fulfillment. Chronicles adds that he brought home Edom's gods and worshiped them (2 Chronicles 25:14).
Read as grace without merit

Jeroboam II's success comes not because he is good but because God has pity on his people (14:26–27). Kings shows God working through bad kings, and Jonah's word of hope prepares for the book in which God has pity even on Nineveh.

views.H: These are the years of Israel's last greatness and Judah's humbling, about 796–753 BC. Amaziah's mercy to his enemies' sons shows that the law of Deuteronomy was known and honored.
views.C: Critical scholars note that the quotation of Deuteronomy 24:16 (14:6) is likely an editor's addition. Some think 14:26–27, with its pity for Israel, was written while the northern kingdom still stood, and others that it is a late reflection on why Israel survived so long.
views.A: The Samaria ostraca, records of wine and oil delivered to the capital, are dated by many to the reign of Jeroboam II, and the prosperity Amos condemns shows in the fine ivories found at Samaria. Excavations at Lachish (14:19) show a great fortress city of this period.
views.J: The rabbis identified Jonah son of Amittai with the son of the widow of Zarephath and with the young prophet who anointed Jehu (Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer; Seder Olam).
views.X: Jonah of Gath-hepher, a town in Galilee, is the prophet whose "sign" Jesus says he will give (Matthew 12:39–41). Christian readers note that the God who rescued an undeserving Israel through Jeroboam is the God who sends Jonah to Nineveh.

deep.b: Jeroboam II's reign produced two very different prophetic words. Jonah son of Amittai promised that Israel's borders would be restored "from Lebo-hamath to the Sea of the Arabah" (14:25). Amos, a farmer from Judah preaching at Bethel in the same reign, said that God would raise a nation to oppress Israel "from Lebo-hamath to the wadi of the Arabah" (Amos 6:14), and that Jeroboam's house would fall by the sword (Amos 7:9–11). Hosea, too, prophesied in his days (Hosea 1:1). Kings records only Jonah's word, fulfilled; the prophetic books record the warnings that were fulfilled thirty years later. Read together, they show how God's mercy and God's judgment can be announced to the same generation.

echoes: Deuteronomy 24:16; Judges 9:8–15; 2 Chronicles 25:1–28; Jonah 1:1; Amos 6:13–14; Amos 7:9–11; Deuteronomy 32:36; Deuteronomy 9:14

settings.what: The law of personal guilt
settings.by: Moses, quoted by the narrator from 'the book of the law of Moses' (Deuteronomy 24:16)
settings.to: Israel's judges and kings, bound to punish only the guilty; here applied by Amaziah
settings.when: When Amaziah executed his father's murderers but spared their sons
settings.why: The law limits revenge to the one who sinned, against the common practice of wiping out a killer's family. Kings quotes it to praise Amaziah for keeping Moses' law. It is one of the few places in Kings that quotes a written law word for word. For exiles it answered the complaint that children were punished for their parents' sins (Ezekiel 18:2).

settings.what: Amaziah's challenge and Jehoash's fable
settings.by: Amaziah king of Judah; then Jehoash king of Israel
settings.to: Each other, by messengers
settings.when: After Amaziah's victory over Edom, about 790 BC
settings.why: Amaziah's 'let us look each other in the face' is a call to battle. Jehoash answers with a fable: a thornbush asks the cedar for a marriage and is trampled. The fable mocks Amaziah's pride and warns him to stay home. In Kings the exchange explains a defeat that broke Jerusalem's wall and emptied the Temple treasury. Readers learn that pride after one victory can ruin a kingdom.

settings.what: Jonah's prophecy and the narrator's reason
settings.by: The LORD, through Jonah son of Amittai of Gath-hepher (reported); then the narrator
settings.to: Israel under Jeroboam II; the narrator's comment is for the readers of Kings
settings.when: Jeroboam II's reign, about 786–746 BC
settings.why: Jonah's words are not given, only that he foretold the winning back of Israel's border. The narrator explains why God helped an evil king: the LORD saw Israel's bitter misery, and he had never spoken of erasing Israel's name. For readers, the passage showed God's pity reaching even a sinful kingdom. It is the same Jonah whose book shows God's pity for Nineveh.

title: Six Kings and a Rising Empire
sum: Azariah (Uzziah) of Judah reigns fifty-two years, but the LORD strikes him with a skin disease and he lives apart while his son Jotham governs. In Israel, Jehu's dynasty ends exactly as promised: Zechariah, the fourth generation, is murdered after six months. Then the kingdom spins apart. Shallum lasts a month; Menahem kills him and pays Pul of Assyria a thousand talents to stay in power; his son Pekahiah is murdered by Pekah; Pekah is murdered by Hoshea.

Behind the palace killings stands Assyria. Tiglath-pileser III takes Galilee and Gilead and deports their people, the first exile of Israelites. In Judah, Jotham builds a temple gate, and the LORD begins to send Rezin of Damascus and Pekah of Israel against Judah, setting the stage for the crisis of Isaiah 7.
readings: Read as the end approaching

The chapter's relentless formulas, "he did what was evil," "plotted against him," "struck him down," show a kingdom without stability, as Hosea said: "They crowned kings, but the choice was not mine" (Hosea 8:4).
Read with the Assyrian records

For historians this is one of the best-documented chapters in the Bible: Tiglath-pileser III's inscriptions name Menahem, Pekah and Hoshea, record tribute and deportations, and help date the reigns, though the figures in Kings do not always fit them.

views.H: These events cover about 792–732 BC. The regnal figures are accurate records once co-regencies (Uzziah and Jotham) and rival reigns (Pekah in Gilead) are recognized, as Thiele argued.
views.C: Critical scholars see a chain of brief notices from royal annals, framed by the editor's formulas. The chronological contradictions (15:1, 15:27, 15:30) show that the figures came from different sources or were miscopied.
views.A: Tiglath-pileser III's annals and a stela from western Iran list "Menahem of Samaria" among his tributaries (about 738 BC). His Summary Inscription says the Israelites overthrew Pekah and he made Hoshea king. Destruction layers at Hazor and other northern sites date to his campaigns of 734–732. A first-century AD plaque in Jerusalem marks the reburial of "Uzziah king of Judah."
views.J: Jewish tradition, following Chronicles and Josephus, explained Uzziah's disease as punishment for burning incense in the temple, and linked it to the earthquake of Amos 1:1. Isaiah's call came in the year King Uzziah died (Isaiah 6:1); the Targum renders it "the year King Uzziah was struck" with his disease, since one with such a disease was counted as dead.
views.X: Isaiah's promise of light for "Galilee of the nations," the land first darkened by Tiglath-pileser's conquest (15:29), is quoted by Matthew when Jesus begins his ministry in Galilee (Matthew 4:13–16).

deep.b: 15:27 gives Pekah twenty years, but Assyrian records show Menahem paying tribute about 738 BC and Pekah dead by 732. Thiele proposed that Pekah ruled a rival kingdom in Gilead from 752, the year Menahem seized Samaria, so that Israel had two kings for twelve years; he pointed to Pekah's Gileadite supporters (15:25) and Hosea's mention of "Israel and Ephraim" (Hosea 5:5). Others suggest Pekah dated his reign from Menahem's accession to deny Menahem's legitimacy. Tadmor and Cogan treat the figure as an error and give Pekah a few years, about 735–732; Albright's system gave 737–732. Galil and Hayes–Hooker build their own reconstructions. The problem shows how much the chronology of the kings depends on choices that scholars make, and it is not solved.

Kings gives Uzziah seven verses and no reason for his disease. Chronicles makes him a great builder and soldier who grew proud, entered the temple to burn incense, and was struck with skin disease on his forehead while the eighty priests who confronted him looked on (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). Josephus adds an earthquake at the moment of his sin (Antiquities 9.10.4). Isaiah dates his vision of the LORD on a high throne to the year Uzziah died (Isaiah 6:1), and many readers have seen a contrast: the earthly king who reached for holiness and was struck, and the heavenly King whose holiness the prophet cannot bear.

echoes: 2 Chronicles 26:1–27:9; Isaiah 6:1; Isaiah 9:1–2; Matthew 4:13–16; Hosea 7:7; Hosea 8:4; Amos 1:1; 1 Chronicles 5:26

title: Ahaz Calls in Assyria
sum: Ahaz of Judah is the first king since Athaliah of whom Kings says flatly that he did not do right. He walks in the way of Israel's kings and even makes his son pass through the fire. When Rezin of Damascus and Pekah of Israel besiege Jerusalem, Ahaz sends Tiglath-pileser of Assyria the temple's silver and gold with a message: "Your servant and your son is what I am." Assyria takes Damascus and kills Rezin.

Ahaz goes to Damascus to meet his new master, sees an altar there and has a copy built in Jerusalem. The LORD's bronze altar is pushed aside, the bronze stands and the Sea are stripped, and the temple is altered "because of the king of Assyria." The chapter shows Judah buying safety at the cost of its independence and its worship.
readings: Read with Isaiah
Isaiah 7 tells the same crisis from the prophet's side: Isaiah urges Ahaz to trust the LORD and offers a sign, Immanuel; Ahaz refuses and turns to Assyria. Kings shows the result of that choice.
Read as cultural surrender

Many scholars read the altar not as an Assyrian demand but as Ahaz's own choice to imitate the powerful. Kings presents it as Judah becoming like the nations, the same charge it will bring against Israel in chapter 17.

views.H: Ahaz reigns about 735–715 BC (Thiele). His appeal to Assyria and his altar are historical acts of unbelief, and his son's sacrifice is real child sacrifice, the sin Deuteronomy most abhors.
views.C: Critical scholars see a priestly source behind the altar account (16:10–18), perhaps more neutral originally, which the Deuteronomistic editor framed with condemnation (16:2–4). Some doubt that "pass through the fire" means sacrifice.
views.A: Tiglath-pileser's Summary Inscription lists "Jehoahaz (Iauhazi) of Judah" among kings who paid him tribute about 734 BC, the Assyrian form of Ahaz's full name. Damascus fell in 732 and became an Assyrian province. An unprovenanced seal impression reading "Ahaz son of Jotham, king of Judah" was published in the 1990s.
views.J: The rabbis counted Ahaz among the worst kings and said he closed the synagogues and schools (Genesis Rabbah 42). The Mishnah's teaching on Molech (Mishnah Sanhedrin 7:7) understood "passing through the fire" as a rite of handing a child over to an idol.
views.X: The Immanuel sign given to Ahaz in this crisis (Isaiah 7:14) is quoted by Matthew of Jesus' birth (Matthew 1:22–23), so this chapter is the historical setting of one of the best-known prophecies in Christian tradition.

deep.b: Was Ahaz forced to copy the altar? Older scholars thought Assyria imposed its religion on vassals. Mordechai Cogan (1974) and John McKay (1973) argued that Assyria did not usually do so to vassal states like Judah, and that the altar was probably of Syrian style. Ahaz kept worshiping the LORD on it, with the regular morning and evening offerings (16:15), but moved the LORD's bronze altar aside and kept it "for me to inquire by." Chronicles goes further and says he sacrificed to the gods of Damascus, shut the temple doors and built altars at every corner of Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 28:23–24). Either way, Kings sees a king reshaping the LORD's house to please a foreign power.

echoes: Isaiah 7:1–17; Isaiah 8:1–8; 2 Chronicles 28:1–27; Deuteronomy 12:31; Deuteronomy 18:10; Amos 1:5; 1 Kings 7:23–39; Matthew 1:22–23

settings.what: Ahaz's appeal to Tiglath-pileser
settings.to: Tiglath-pileser III king of Assyria
settings.when: When Rezin of Aram and Pekah of Israel besieged Jerusalem, about 734 BC
settings.why: 'I am your servant and your son. Come up! Save me.' Ahaz gives himself as a vassal and pays with Temple silver. The words use the language a king of David's line should use only of the LORD. Kings shows readers the moment Judah traded trust in the LORD for Assyria's protection, against Isaiah's advice (Isaiah 7).

settings.what: Ahaz's order on the new altar
settings.to: Uriah the priest
settings.when: After Ahaz returned from meeting Tiglath-pileser in Damascus
settings.why: A royal order changing Temple worship. All the daily, royal and public offerings go on the new altar modeled on the one in Damascus. The old bronze altar is kept for the king's inquiry. It shows a king of David's line rearranging the LORD's house to please a foreign overlord. Readers see how loyalty to an empire reached into worship.
views: Some historians thought Assyria imposed its worship on vassals.
Most scholars now, following Cogan, think Assyria did not require it, and Ahaz chose to copy a Damascus model.

title: The End of Israel
sum: Hoshea, the last king of Israel, pays tribute to Shalmaneser of Assyria, then turns to Egypt and stops paying. Assyria arrests him, besieges Samaria for three years and takes it, about 722 BC. The people are deported to Upper Mesopotamia and Media. Then the narrator stops the story to preach: Israel fell because it feared other gods, ignored every prophet, made calves and Asherah poles, burned its children and "went after vapor and became vapor." Judah, it warns, has walked the same road.

The last section tells what came next. The king of Assyria settles peoples from Babylon, Cuthah, Hamath and elsewhere in Samaria. Lions attack them, so an Israelite priest is sent back to Bethel to teach "the ways of the god of the land." The newcomers fear the LORD and serve their own gods too, "to this day." Jews long read this as the origin of the Samaritans, who tell their own story very differently.
readings: Read as covenant judgment
The fall of Samaria is the curse of Deuteronomy coming true: the LORD himself removed Israel from his sight (17:18, 17:23). The sermon of 17:7–23 is the theological center of Kings.
Read as imperial history

Historians see the end of a small state that rebelled against the world's greatest empire. Assyrian records name Shalmaneser V and Sargon II, count the deportees and describe the resettlement, confirming the outline of Kings.
Read as a contested origin story
17:24–41 is a Judean account of northern neighbors. The Samaritans, who still worship at Mount Gerizim, say they descend from Israelites who stayed in the land and kept the law faithfully.

views.H: Samaria fell in 722 BC after a three-year siege. Traditional Jewish and Christian readers take 17:7–23 as the inspired verdict of a prophetic historian (Jeremiah, in Jewish tradition), and 17:24–41 as the history of the mixed population later called Samaritans.
views.C: Most critical scholars see the sermon as Deuteronomistic, with additions about Judah (17:13, 17:19–20) written after 586 BC, and 17:24–41 as growing in stages, with its sharpest polemic coming from Persian-period quarrels between Jerusalem and Samaria.
views.A: The Babylonian Chronicle says Shalmaneser V "ravaged Samaria." Sargon II claims: "I besieged and conquered Samaria" and carried off 27,290 people, formed fifty chariots from them, and settled others there; his records also mention Arabs settled in Samaria about 715. Documents from Gozan and other sites include Israelite names.
views.J: The rabbis called the Samaritans Kutim, after Cuthah (17:24), and debated whether they were "lion converts" (Bavli Kiddushin 75b). Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Eliezer debated whether the ten tribes would ever return (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:3). The Samaritans' own chronicles trace their line to Joseph's tribes.
views.X: Jesus' meeting with the Samaritan woman (John 4) and his parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:30–37) reach across the divide this chapter describes. Christian readers have also seen in Israel's fall a warning against mixing faith in God with other loyalties (17:33, 17:41).

deep.b: Kings says "the king of Assyria" took Samaria in Hoshea's ninth year, right after naming Shalmaneser (17:3–6; 18:9–10). The Babylonian Chronicle credits Shalmaneser V with ravaging "Shamara'in." Sargon II, who came to the throne in late 722, boasts in several inscriptions that he conquered Samaria and deported 27,290 people. Hayim Tadmor's widely followed solution is that Shalmaneser took the city in 722, just before his death, and that Sargon put down a revolt there in 720 and carried out the deportation and resettlement. Bob Becking and others have proposed variations. All agree that the northern kingdom ended between 722 and 720 BC.

Kings presents the people of Samaria after 722 as foreign settlers with a mixed religion. The Samaritans see it differently. They call themselves Shamerim, "keepers" of the Law of Moses, and trace their descent to Ephraim and Manasseh, sons of Joseph, and to priests of the line of Aaron. In their chronicles, such as that of Abu'l-Fath (fourteenth century), the break came long before Assyria, when the priest Eli left the true sanctuary on Mount Gerizim (Deuteronomy 11:29; Deuteronomy 27:4–13 in their Pentateuch) and set up a rival one at Shiloh. They regard Judaism as the breakaway. Most historians think the truth lies between: Assyria deported many but not all Israelites (2 Chronicles 30:1–11), foreigners were settled, and the decisive split came in the Persian and Hellenistic periods, around the Gerizim temple built in the fifth century BC and destroyed by John Hyrcanus about 110 BC. Genetic studies of the modern community find ancestry close to other Israelite populations. About nine hundred Samaritans live today at Mount Gerizim and in Holon.

deep.title: Claude's theory: "fear" as the key word of 17:24–41
deep.b: This is my own reading, though the importance of "fear" here is widely noticed. The verb yare', "fear," appears eleven times in 17:25–41. The settlers first do not fear the LORD (17:25), then learn to fear him (17:28, 17:32–33), and yet are said not to fear him (17:34), because the covenant demands fearing the LORD and no other gods (17:35–39). I suggest the passage is built as a definition by contrast: "fear of the LORD" that sits alongside other fears is not fear of the LORD at all. That would explain the apparent contradiction, and it makes the passage less an attack on one people than a closing lesson for every reader of Kings, including Judah (17:19).

echoes: Deuteronomy 28:36; Deuteronomy 28:64; Deuteronomy 29:28; 1 Kings 12:26–33; 1 Kings 14:15–16; Jeremiah 2:5; Hosea 7:11; Ezra 4:1–10; John 4:9–26; Luke 10:30–37

settings.what: The sermon on why Israel fell
settings.to: The readers of Kings: Judeans who had seen Samaria fall, and later exiles from Judah in Babylon
settings.when: Placed right after the fall of Samaria in 722 BC, but written for a later generation
settings.why: Not a speech in the story but the narrator stopping it to preach. It lists Israel's sins (other gods, high places, calves, Asherah, child sacrifice, divination) and the prophets' warnings ignored, and it says Judah walked the same road (17:13, 19). The sermon was meant to make readers see the fall of the north as a lesson about themselves. Read in the exile, it explains Judah's fall too, and its call to 'turn back' (17:13) is still the way open to them.
views: Cross and others: the core was written under Josiah, to warn Judah and support his reform and his claim on the north; 17:19–20 was added in the exile.
Noth and others: the whole sermon belongs to the exilic history and explains both falls at once.
Traditional readers: the voice of a prophet such as Jeremiah, drawing the lesson from history for his own generation.

settings.what: The report to the king of Assyria and his order
settings.by: Officials in Samaria; then the king of Assyria
settings.to: The king of Assyria; then his officials
settings.when: After the new settlers in Samaria were attacked by lions
settings.why: The settlers' complaint uses the ancient idea that every land has its god, who must be served in the right way. The king's order sends back an Israelite priest to teach them. The result is a mixed worship (17:33). For Judean readers the passage explained the origins of the people living in the north, a question that mattered after the exile (Ezra 4:2).

settings.what: The second sermon, quoting the covenant
settings.by: The narrator of Kings, quoting the LORD's covenant commands
settings.to: The readers of Kings, about the mixed peoples of Samaria 'to this day'
settings.when: In the writer's own time, long after 722 BC
settings.why: The narrator quotes the covenant given to 'the sons of Jacob' (17:35–39): fear the LORD only, not other gods. He judges the settlers' worship as not truly fearing the LORD at all. The passage warns readers that serving the LORD alongside other gods is not serving him. Later disputes between Jews and Samaritans drew on it.
views: Most commentators: 17:34–41 judges the foreign settlers and their descendants.
Some scholars think part of it (17:34b–40) first spoke of the remaining Israelites, who 'did not listen.'
